summary: Verapamil is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for angina, supraventricular arrhythmias (PSVT, atrial fibrillation/flutter rate control), and hypertension. Immediate-release dosing is typically 80-120 mg three times daily, not to exceed 480 mg/day. Its negative inotropic and dromotropic effects limit use in heart failure and AV block, and it raises levels of digoxin and CYP3A4-substrate statins.
indications: Angina at rest including vasospastic (Prinzmetal's variant) and unstable (crescendo, pre-infarction) angina
Control of ventricular rate (with digitalis) in chronic atrial flutter and/or atrial fibrillation
Prophylaxis of repetitive paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)

moa: Verapamil is a calcium ion influx inhibitor (slow-channel blocker) that modulates the influx of ionic calcium across the cell membrane of arterial smooth muscle and of cardiac conductile and contractile cells. It dilates coronary and peripheral arteries (reducing afterload and relieving spasm) and, by decreasing calcium influx through the AV node, prolongs the AV nodal effective refractory period and slows AV conduction, slowing ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation/flutter and terminating PSVT.

absolute: Hypotension (systolic <90 mm Hg) or cardiogenic shock
Second- or third-degree AV block (unless functioning pacemaker)
Atrial flutter/fibrillation with an accessory bypass tract (WPW, Lown-Ganong-Levine)
relative: Mild to moderate heart failure or any ventricular dysfunction with concurrent beta-blocker

preg: Former Pregnancy Category C. Animal reproduction studies revealed no teratogenicity, but high multiples were embryocidal and retarded fetal growth (likely from maternal effects). There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Verapamil crosses the placenta and is detectable in umbilical vein blood at delivery.
lact: Verapamil is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for adverse reactions in nursing infants, nursing should be discontinued while verapamil is administered.
renal: About 70% of a dose is excreted as metabolites in urine. Verapamil is not removed by hemodialysis. Administer cautiously to patients with impaired renal function and monitor for abnormal PR-interval prolongation or other signs of overdose.
hepatic: Verapamil is highly metabolized by the liver; severe liver dysfunction prolongs the elimination half-life to about 14 to 16 hours. Give approximately 30% of the normal daily dose and monitor closely for PR-interval prolongation and other excessive pharmacologic effects.

major: Beta-blockers - additive negative effects on heart rate, AV conduction, and contractility; avoid in AV conduction abnormalities or depressed LV function
Digoxin - chronic verapamil raises serum digoxin 50-75% in first week; reduce digoxin dose to avoid toxicity
Simvastatin/lovastatin (CYP3A4-substrate statins) - myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk; limit simvastatin to 10 mg/day and lovastatin to 40 mg/day
Disopyramide - avoid within 48 h before or 24 h after verapamil; flecainide - additive negative inotropy and AV conduction prolongation
moderate: CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, ritonavir) - raise verapamil levels; CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, phenobarbital) - lower verapamil levels
Other CYP3A4 substrates (atorvastatin) - may require lower starting/maintenance doses
Carbamazepine - verapamil raises levels (diplopia, ataxia, dizziness)
Lithium - altered levels and possible neurotoxicity
Clonidine - sinus bradycardia; monitor heart rate
Antihypertensives and alpha-blockers (prazosin) - additive BP lowering
Neuromuscular blockers and inhalation anesthetics - potentiated effects/cardiovascular depression
minor: Aspirin - increased bleeding times beyond aspirin alone
Cimetidine - variable effect on verapamil clearance
Nitrates - beneficial interaction, no undesirable effects
Quinidine - hypotension in IHSS; increased quinidine levels
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice may increase verapamil plasma levels; otherwise may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Verapamil may increase blood alcohol concentrations and prolong its effects.
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong the PR interval on ECG and elevate liver transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin.

rare: Rapid ventricular response/fibrillation in accessory bypass tract
emergency: Acute pulmonary edema in severe LV dysfunction

monitoring: ECG for PR-interval prolongation and AV block, especially during early titration
Serum digoxin levels when used concomitantly
Signs of worsening heart failure in patients with ventricular dysfunction
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed; do not stop abruptly without medical advice
Constipation is common - increase fiber and fluids as advised
Avoid grapefruit juice and limit alcohol
Report swelling, shortness of breath, slow heartbeat, fainting, or dizziness
Inform all providers you take verapamil, especially before starting a statin or if taking digoxin
pk: Dosed three to four times daily (IR)
pearls: Negative inotrope - avoid in HFrEF (EF <30%) and with beta-blockers in LV dysfunction
Raises serum digoxin 50-75%; reduce digoxin dose
Limit simvastatin to 10 mg/day and lovastatin to 40 mg/day when combined

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Treat all verapamil overdoses as serious and observe at least 48 hours, preferably under continuous hospital care (delayed effects with extended-release). Overdose causes hypotension and bradycardia. Treatment is supportive: parenteral calcium solutions (e.g., calcium chloride), beta-adrenergic stimulation, vasopressors, atropine, and cardiac pacing for high-degree AV block; treat asystole with CPR. Verapamil cannot be removed by hemodialysis.
